note: Recycling rules differ between councils. Steps describe common practice; the app tells users to check local rules.

steps: Empty the bottle and give it a quick rinse.
Squash it to save space. Check your local rules on whether to keep the cap on.
Put it in the plastics or mixed recycling bin.

upcycling.title: Self-watering planter
steps: Cut the bottle in half around the middle.
Push a cotton string through a small hole in the cap so it hangs into the bottom half.
Turn the top half upside down into the bottom, add water below and soil plus a plant on top.
precautions: Cut slowly and away from your body. Ask an adult to help with scissors.

steps: Empty it fully and rinse out any sugary drink.
Squash it, and follow local rules on keeping the cap on.
Put it in the plastics or mixed recycling bin.

upcycling.title: Hanging bird feeder
steps: Make two small holes on opposite sides near the bottom and push a wooden spoon through them.
Repeat a little higher with the second spoon, then enlarge the holes above each spoon slightly so seed can trickle out.
Fill the bottle with seed, tie string around the neck and hang it from a branch.
precautions: Ask an adult to make the holes with a craft knife or scissors.

steps: Rinse well, because milk residue smells and contaminates other recycling.
Squash it flat and follow local rules for the cap.
Put it in the plastics or mixed recycling bin.

upcycling.title: Garden watering can
steps: Wash the jug and cap with warm soapy water.
Press a thumbtack through the cap 8 to 10 times to make small holes.
Fill the jug with water, screw on the cap and tip it gently over your plants.
precautions: Push the pin into the cap on a table, not in your hand.

recycling.accepted: Usually accepted in household recycling once empty.
steps: Use it up completely and rinse out the soap.
Remove the pump if it has one, because pumps contain metal springs and usually go in general waste.
Put the bottle and cap in the plastics or mixed recycling bin.

upcycling.title: Desk or bathroom tidy
steps: Rinse the bottle until no soap foams, then let it dry.
Cut off the top third so you have an open pot.
Cover the cut edge with tape, decorate it and use it for pens, brushes or hair ties.
precautions: Do not reuse bottles that held bleach or strong cleaners.
Do not store food in it.

recycling.accepted: Accepted in many areas. Check your council's list for pots, tubs and trays.
steps: Scrape out leftovers and rinse.
Peel off the foil lid and recycle it with metals if your area accepts foil.
Put the cup in the plastics recycling if pots are accepted, otherwise in general waste.

upcycling.title: Seed starter pots
steps: Poke two or three small drainage holes in the bottom with a pencil.
Fill each cup with soil and plant two seeds about 1 cm deep.
Stand the cups on a tray by a sunny window and water a little every few days.
precautions: Wash your hands after handling soil.

recycling.accepted: Accepted in many areas when clean.
steps: Remove all food and wipe out grease.
Rinse with warm water and let it dry.
Put it in the plastics recycling if tubs are accepted. Heavily greasy containers go in general waste.

upcycling.title: Drawer organiser
materials: Several clean containers of different sizes
steps: Wash the containers and lids and let them dry.
Arrange them inside a drawer to fit the space.
Stick them down with double-sided tape and sort small items such as cables, batteries or stationery into them.

recycling.accepted: Loose caps are often too small for sorting machines.
steps: Check your local rules: many areas ask you to screw the cap back on the empty bottle.
If loose caps are not accepted, collect them for a cap collection scheme if one exists near you.
Otherwise put loose caps in general waste.

upcycling.title: Bottle-cap coasters
steps: Wash and dry the caps and sort them by colour.
Arrange them flat-side up on the cork circle in a pattern.
Glue each cap down and leave it to dry overnight before use.
precautions: Keep caps away from small children; they are a choking hazard.

recycling.accepted: Usually not accepted in household bins because film jams sorting machines.
steps: Reuse it as many times as you can.
Make sure it is empty, clean and dry.
Take it to a supermarket soft-plastics or bag collection point.

upcycling.title: Plastic yarn (plarn) braid
steps: Flatten each bag and cut it into 3 cm wide loops across the bag.
Link the loops together into one long strip by pulling each loop through the next.
Tape three strips to a table and braid them into a strong rope for skipping, tying or weaving.
precautions: Keep plastic bags away from babies and small children.

recycling.accepted: Not recyclable in most household bins because straws are too small to sort.
steps: Avoid single-use straws where you can.
Collect used straws for a craft project.
Otherwise put them in general waste, not the recycling.

upcycling.title: Straw pencil holder
materials: An empty can or cardboard tube
steps: Wash and dry the straws and cut them to the height of the can.
Spread glue around the outside of the can in strips.
Press the straws side by side around the can until it is covered, then let it dry.
precautions: Cover any sharp rim of the can with tape first.

recycling.accepted: Clear PET (1) cups are often accepted; PS (6) cups usually are not.
steps: Look for the number inside the triangle on the bottom of the cup.
If it is 1, rinse it and put it in the plastics recycling.
If it is 6 or has no number, put it in general waste.

upcycling.title: Mini herb planter
steps: Poke drainage holes in the bottom of each cup with a pencil.
Add a layer of small stones, then fill with soil.
Sow herb seeds such as cress or basil and keep the soil damp on a sunny sill.
Remove tape and labels and keep it clean.
Check whether your council or a local shop has a foam drop-off point.
If not, break it into pieces in a bag and put it in general waste so it does not blow away.

upcycling.title: Plant-pot drainage filler
steps: Break the foam into chunks about the size of a walnut, inside a bag to catch the bits.
Fill the bottom quarter of a large pot with the chunks.
Add soil on top and plant as normal. The foam makes the pot lighter and drains well.
precautions: Do not use foam that touched raw meat.

recycling.accepted: Not accepted in household recycling because the layers cannot be separated.
steps: Shake out crumbs and wipe the inside.
Check for a take-back or soft-plastics scheme at local shops.
If there is none, put it in general waste.

upcycling.title: Woven coaster
steps: Cut each packet open, wash and dry it, and cut it into 2 cm strips.
Fold each strip in half lengthways so the shiny side shows.
Weave the strips over and under into a square and tape the edges on the back.

recycling.accepted: Usually not accepted in household recycling.
steps: Reuse it at home or in packed lunches where you can.
Wash it if you plan to use it for crafts.
Otherwise put it in general waste.

upcycling.title: Garden plant labels
steps: Wash and dry the cutlery.
Write the plant name on the flat part with a permanent marker.
Push the handle into the soil next to each plant.

recycling.accepted: Accepted in many areas as pots, tubs and trays.
steps: Remove the absorbent pad and the label if they peel off easily.
Rinse out juice and let it dry.
Put it in the plastics recycling if trays are accepted in your area.

upcycling.title: Mini greenhouse for seedlings
steps: Fill the bottom of the punnet with 3 cm of damp soil.
Sprinkle seeds on top and cover lightly with soil.
Close the lid to keep moisture in, place it in light, and open it once seedlings touch the lid.
